"Solar System for Junior Astronauts" is a real-time interactive 3D solar system simulator built in Rust using the Bevy game engine, capable of running natively on desktop and inside web browsers via WebAssembly

The project addresses the challenge of making complex astronomy and orbital mechanics engaging and accessible for children. It solves this by combining robust Kepler-style elliptical orbits and accurate astronomical data with a playful, intuitive, and bilingual interface available in both English and Spanish. Users can seamlessly explore 24 celestial bodies, freely control the simulation clock, switch between true scales and real-date modes, and learn through information cards, fun facts, interactive quizzes, and an AI-powered space guide named Dopply.

This project matters because it successfully merges modern, high-performance software engineering—featuring a clean Entity Component System (ECS) architecture, immediate-mode gizmos, and non-blocking asynchronous AI background requests—with early science education. By ensuring that background tasks like AI responses never freeze the simulation loop, it delivers a smooth, immersive, and educational experience across modest hardware and web platforms alike.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Solar System for Junior Astronauts is a real-time 3D simulator of the Solar System designed especially for kids, functioning as an interactive planetarium where 24 celestial bodies can be explored, including the Sun, the 8 planets, the Moon, the moons of Mars and Jupiter, Titan, Triton, three dwarf planets, Halley's Comet, and the two Voyager probes. The program allows users to navigate using the mouse and keyboard, control time by pausing, speeding up, slowing down, or jumping forward and backward on the calendar, use special modes like real dates, real scale, and size comparison, and learn through information cards, quizzes, and an AI-powered space guide named Dopply. Internally, the software is built on the ECS (Entity Component System) architecture of the Bevy game engine, organizing data into components and executing logic in systems divided into four chained stages: Sim, SimLate, Visual, and Overlay. Orbits are computed in an elliptical Kepler-style, real-date positions are derived from the J2000 epoch, and scale transitions use logarithmic interpolation

What benefits does it have?

The project offers major educational and interactive benefits by facilitating self-guided learning through guided tours, fun facts, a quiz system, and visual aids such as shadows for eclipses and orbital trails. Additionally, it stands out for being fully bilingual, allowing users to dynamically switch between Spanish and English across the entire interface without needing to restart the program. It is also optimized to run smoothly on modest hardware thanks to its three graphical quality levels (low, medium, high).

What is the expected impact of the project?

The expected impact is to serve as a modern and engaging pedagogical tool that sparks children's interest in astronomy and science, allowing them to intuitively, visually, and playfully understand complex space concepts such as distances, scales, orbits, and the movement of celestial bodies.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software were used to develop your project?

The application was developed using the Rust programming language alongside the Bevy game engine (version 0.20). The program is capable of running both as a native desktop application and in the web browser by compiling to WebAssembly. For graphics and visuals, surface textures from Solar System Scope (under a CC BY 4.0 license) and the Instrument Sans typography were used, achieving efficient performance even on modest hardware.

How is your project creative?

The creativity of the project lies in its innovative combination of rigorous mathematical and astronomical simulation—such as the true positions of planets and the physical behavior of the comet's tail always pointing away from the Sun—with a child-friendly and accessible interface. Particularly noteworthy is the integration of "Dopply," an artificial intelligence assistant connected via asynchronous channels that handles chats and generates interactive quizzes in real time without freezing or affecting the 3D animation's performance. Furthermore, its visualization system is creative, allowing seamless switching between an aesthetic view and real scales using logarithmic interpolation, alongside lining bodies up side by side for easy visual comparison.

What factors did your team consider?

During development, critical factors such as performance and fluidity were considered, ensuring that AI requests were processed off the main rendering thread to prevent freezes or stutters in the animation. Cross-platform compatibility was also anticipated by accounting for architectural differences between the desktop environment and the web to guarantee the correct loading of assets. Finally, to ensure software robustness, generation numbers were implemented in quizzes to prevent late replies from earlier requests from overwriting the current state, while also unifying keyboard and mouse actions into a single event queue.
